story: A god named Ríg wandered along a seashore and came to a farm-hut owned by a couple called Ái and Edda, who gave him poor food and let him sleep between them in their bed. Nine months later Edda bore a dark, ugly son named Þræll, who married a woman named Thír; their many sons and daughters became the race of serfs. Traveling on, Ríg reached a better house belonging to Afi and Amma, who fed him well and likewise let him sleep between them. Nine months later a ruddy son, Karl, was born; he married a woman named Snör, and their children became free farmers, craftsmen, and herdsmen. Continuing further, Ríg came to a splendid mansion of Faðir and Móðir, who served him a magnificent meal. Nine months later a beautiful, fair-haired son, Jarl, was born. When Jarl grew skilled with weapons, hawks, hounds, and horses, Ríg returned, claimed him as his son, gave him his own name, taught him runes, and urged him toward lordship. Jarl won eighteen homesteads through war and married Erna, daughter of a lord named Hersir; they had twelve sons, ancestors of the warrior nobility. The youngest, Konr, surpassed all others in rune-lore, magic, understanding birds' speech, quenching fire, and healing minds, and inherited the name Ríg as well. While hunting birds in a forest, Konr was told by a crow that he should instead make war and seek the halls of two rulers, Dan and Danþír, who were wealthier than he. The poem breaks off at this point.
blind: A wandering deity walked along a shoreline and came to a hut owned by an elderly couple, who gave him poor food and let him sleep between them in their bed. Nine months later the woman bore a dark, ugly son, who married another woman; their many sons and daughters became a class of servants. Traveling on, the deity reached a better house belonging to a second couple, who fed him well and likewise let him sleep between them. Nine months later a ruddy son was born; he married a woman, and their children became free farmers, craftsmen, and herders. Continuing further, the deity came to a splendid mansion belonging to a third couple, who served him a magnificent meal. Nine months later a beautiful, fair-haired son was born. When this son grew skilled with weapons, hunting birds, hounds, and horses, the deity returned, claimed him as his own child, gave him his own title, taught him secret knowledge, and urged him toward lordship. This son won eighteen homesteads through war and married a noblewoman, daughter of a local lord; they had twelve sons, ancestors of a warrior nobility. The youngest of these sons surpassed all others in secret knowledge, magic, understanding the speech of birds, quenching fire, and healing minds, and inherited his father's title as well. While hunting birds in a forest, he was told by a crow that he should instead make war and seek the halls of two rulers who were wealthier than he. The story breaks off at this point.
